summary.text: At the step corresponding to \(n=7\), \(a(5)=171\) is divisible by \(19\), while a direct computation gives \(a(6)\equiv3\pmod{18}\). Since \(2^{18}\equiv1\pmod{19}\), the required numerator is \(2^{a(6)}+1\equiv2^3+1=9\not\equiv0\pmod{19}\), so it cannot be divisible by \(171\).

full_proof.text:
Let the sequence be defined by
\[
a(1)=a(2)=1,\qquad a(n)=\frac{2^{a(n-1)}+1}{a(n-2)}\quad(n\geq 3).
\]
We will show that the first six terms are integers but that the seventh term is not. Thus the assertion that every term is an integer is false.

The first few applications of the recurrence give
\[
a(3)=\frac{2^{a(2)}+1}{a(1)}=\frac{2^1+1}{1}=3,
\]
\[
a(4)=\frac{2^{a(3)}+1}{a(2)}=\frac{2^3+1}{1}=9,
\]
and
\[
a(5)=\frac{2^{a(4)}+1}{a(3)}=\frac{2^9+1}{3}
      =\frac{513}{3}=171.
\]
In particular,
\[
a(5)=171=9\cdot 19.
\]

At the next step, set
\[
N:=a(6)=\frac{2^{171}+1}{9}.
\]
This is indeed an integer. To see this directly, work modulo 9. Since
\[
2^6=64\equiv 1\pmod 9
\]
and \(171=6\cdot 28+3\), we have
\[
2^{171}\equiv 2^3=8\equiv -1\pmod 9.
\]
Consequently \(9\mid 2^{171}+1\), so the displayed quotient defining \(N\) is integral. Its decimal value is
\[
N=332572817028187686275682948600327513806149983112761,
\]
although the proof below only needs its residue modulo 18.

We now establish the crucial congruence
\[
N\equiv 3\pmod {18}.
\]
First compute modulo 81. Since \(2\) is relatively prime to \(81\) and
\[
\varphi(81)=81-27=54,
\]
Euler's theorem gives
\[
2^{54}\equiv 1\pmod {81}.
\]
As \(171=3\cdot 54+9\), it follows that
\[
2^{171}=(2^{54})^3 2^9\equiv 2^9=512\equiv 26\pmod {81}.
\]
Therefore
\[
9N=2^{171}+1\equiv 27\pmod {81}.
\]
Equivalently, \(81\mid 9N-27=9(N-3)\). Cancelling the factor 9 in this integer divisibility relation shows that
\[
9\mid N-3,
\]
so \(N\equiv 3\pmod 9\).

Moreover, \(9N=2^{171}+1\) is odd, and hence \(N\) is odd. Write \(N=3+9k\). Since both \(N\) and 3 are odd, \(9k=N-3\) is even. As 9 is odd, \(k\) must be even, say \(k=2j\). Thus
\[
N=3+18j,
\]
which proves \(N\equiv 3\pmod {18}\).

We now examine the numerator that would be used to define the seventh term. Fermat's little theorem modulo 19 gives
\[
2^{18}\equiv 1\pmod {19},
\]
because 19 is prime and is coprime to 2. Since \(N\equiv 3\pmod {18}\), write \(N=18j+3\). Then
\[
2^N+1=2^{18j+3}+1=(2^{18})^j2^3+1
       \equiv 1^j\cdot 8+1
       =9\pmod {19}.
\]
In particular,
\[
19\nmid 2^N+1,
\]
because 9 is not congruent to 0 modulo 19.

On the other hand, the recurrence would require
\[
a(7)=\frac{2^{a(6)}+1}{a(5)}
     =\frac{2^N+1}{171}.
\]
If this were an integer, then \(171\mid 2^N+1\). But \(19\mid171\), so this divisibility would force \(19\mid 2^N+1\), contradicting the congruence
\[
2^N+1\equiv9\pmod {19}.
\]
Therefore \(171\nmid 2^N+1\), and hence \(a(7)\) is not an integer.

Thus the recurrence produces the integral terms
\[
1,\ 1,\ 3,\ 9,\ 171,\ N
\]
through its sixth step, but fails to produce an integer at the seventh step. This disproves the conjecture that every term \(a(n)\) is an integer.
